directorStatement.audienceFeeling: It feels awful when you say something wrong and everyone hears it. Even after class moves on, your stomach can still feel stuck in the bad moment.
directorStatement.emotionalChange: Let the audience feel the blush before the magic begins: embarrassment as a physical freeze, not a lesson. Keep this quiet and recognisable; the drama is in the mismatch between Jenny’s nod and the truth of her posture.
directorStatement.theLaugh: Jenny wants to read the sentence correctly and get safely through her turn. Jenny wants the moment to be over and for nobody to look closely at her hurt. She needs to know that a visible mistake does not reduce her worth. She needs permission to admit she is not all right without becoming the mistake.
directorStatement.visualSurprise: Jenny stands in the exposed classroom space and tries to read the line. The ordinary word on the board becomes dangerous through silence, hesitation and the accidental wrong word. The tiny laugh is not cruelly staged, but it is enough to make Jenny’s body close around the worksheet and make her corr -> Jenny holding her bag, the folded worksheet hidden inside.
directorStatement.carryForward: Jenny has hidden the feeling instead of sharing it, carrying the shame forward.

northStar.surfaceStory: Jenny is asked to read aloud. The word on the board trips her, the room goes very still, and the mistake feels bigger than the classroom. She wants the moment to pass without being seen in it.
northStar.universalTruth: A small mistake can feel like it changes how others see you, especially when everyone is looking.
northStar.childClearWant: Jenny wants to get the word right and stop the attention before it sticks.
northStar.emotionalNeed: To feel that being wrong is survivable and does not make her small.
northStar.falseBeliefUnderPressure: If I say the wrong thing, everyone will remember only that.
northStar.relationshipEngine: The teacher’s steady kindness gives Jenny a way back, while the nearby classmate’s simple check-in shows that connection can survive embarrassment.
northStar.ordinaryLifeTruth: When you are put on the spot, your body can close up faster than your thinking can catch up.
northStar.sceneTurn: The mistake moves from being a public problem to something Jenny can answer again, with support still present.
audienceJourney: Recognition: that horrible quiet when a word gets stuck
Tension: the body tightening around the page
Relief: an adult does not make the moment worse
Shift: the wrong answer is not treated as the whole story
Aftertaste: shaky, but no longer alone
northStar.finalAfterFeeling: A little embarrassed, but steadier and more able to try again.
northStar.dialogueSubtractionOpportunity: Let silence, the paper grip, and the tiny pause carry the shame; the dialogue can stay plain and brief.
northStar.environmentPressure: The classroom’s exposed front space, the quiet of the room, and the waiting eyes turn an ordinary reading into pressure.

[Opening Stage]
Create a playable 16:9 opening for S1.SH02; frame-one anticipation, not portrait or payoff.

[Intended Read]
A quiet desk-level classroom opening frame that isolates Jenny in her embarrassed aftermath, with the room still active around her but no Classmate staged yet.

[References]
- Project-stable slots: @图1=Jenny; @图2=scene plate. Never swap roles.

[Frame]

Desk-center placement with Jenny seated at her desk in the classroom interior.
Camera looks from within the room at seated student eye level, aligned to the desk plane.
Leave a clear side lane beside Jenny for the later off-frame classmate check-in.
Keep the front wall, windows, chalkboard, and surrounding desks readable as classroom context without stealing attention from the desk action.
Reserve visible space near Jenny’s bag-hand side for the eventual paper-to-bag concealment path.

Hold empty space frame-right for the classmate’s later approach from outside the opening frame.
Keep a clear low path near Jenny’s bag-side hand for the paper-to-bag concealment movement.
Leave some air above the desk line so the classroom can feel present without crowding Jenny.

[Canonical Style]
Feature-quality stylized 3D CGI. Plush character materials with subsurface scattering; soft fur with individual strands catching the light; glossy eyes with bright catchlights; translucent wing membranes where light passes through. Warm amber key light with cool blue fill and a soft rim light; teal-orange cinematic grade. Shallow depth of field with soft bokeh, gentle ambient occlusion, subtle film grain. [Camera]
Modestly intimate lens relationship at desk level, natural perspective, slight compression of classroom bustle behind Jenny, mostly still camera with no dramatic push. Frame one should feel grounded and ordinary, not stylized or floating.

Steady classroom daylight with a slightly cooler, flatter aftertaste that matches the embarrassed pause. Foreground Jenny is crisp; the background classroom softens gently so the desk action and concealment read first.

Keep every subject grounded in the authored perspective and depth. Match the approved light direction and scale; preserve natural contact shadows, surface reflections and occlusion where subjects meet the environment.

[Performance Freedom]
Animation owns performance, movement, recovery and camera evolution.

Preserve Jenny’s hands and worksheet visibility so concealment can read physically later.

No portrait, locked extreme action pose or payoff, identity or scale drift, changed accessories, omitted reference features, duplicates, anatomy errors, text or watermark. No extra cast, props, body-mounted bags, sacks, baskets or dangling loads. Preserve the locked Scene Look.

inputs.logline: After Jenny hides the shame of misreading a word, Patch leads the Box Monsters into a shoebox classroom where a giant mistake must become something she can try again with, not something that makes her small.

orderedEvents.text: Jenny stands at the front of the classroom holding her worksheet.
The word BRIDGE is written on the board.
Jenny looks at the word. Her fingers tighten around the paper.
One child lets out a tiny laugh. Another child laughs because the first one did.
Jenny looks at the word again. It feels much bigger now.
Final Frame: Jenny frozen, embarrassed, holding the worksheet close.

beats.storyBeat: Jenny stands in the exposed classroom space and tries to read the line. The ordinary word on the board becomes dangerous through silence, hesitation and the accidental wrong word. The tiny laugh is not cruelly staged, but it is enough to make Jenny’s body close around the worksheet and make her corrected answer come out small.
beats.want: Jenny wants to read the sentence correctly and get safely through her turn.
beats.need: She needs to know that a visible mistake does not reduce her worth.
beats.kidRead: It feels awful when you say something wrong and everyone hears it.
beats.adultRead: A small public stumble can become disproportionately huge inside a sensitive child, even when the adults respond gently.
beats.emotionalIntent: Let the audience feel the blush before the magic begins: embarrassment as a physical freeze, not a lesson.
